cells.tense: You are picking what to pass on, here, and you mean it.
cells.ask: Offer one more piece of what matters to you than feels safe — at a table, in a message, spoken. Then watch what it does.
cells.core:
You decide what gets passed on, and you decide it from where you stand. Not the loudest voice and not a passenger — this and not that, said plainly, and saying it is how you pick.

The practices you hand over arrive with your name on them, and they land because of that. What keeps them landing is holding the shape while people push back. That holding is usually done quietly, and it costs a little each time; it is what your evenness is made of. This being yours might look like something you inherited. It isn't — you keep re-choosing it.
cells.sheetLine: You choose what gets passed on, and you own the call.
cells.verb: to pick the direction, this and not that
cells.place: in the shared meanings and practices handed between people

cells.tense: You are bracing for how it all lands at a future you keep trying to write in.
cells.ask: Let one answer sit unanswered this week, even when the quiet gets uncomfortable. Then leave it there.
cells.core:
You shove what you know at people harder than anyone asked. Ahead of you is a version where they finally get it, and you're living in that version — so each exchange becomes a chance to land the point.

What you steer is what gets shared, and this is how it bends: the care turns into control. You start arranging the outcome instead of tending what's in the room. Notice how much of the work is propping up something that hasn't fallen. The shoving buys you distance from the people who would have been on your side. You still know how to pick a direction; the picking just raced ahead of anything you could hold.
cells.sheetLine: Straining a future you can't write has replaced the sharing.
cells.verb: to pick the direction, this and not that

cells.tense: You stopped choosing back there — right at a door you still stand beside.
cells.ask: Take one thing you carry to one person, in an ordinary sentence, and say where it came from. Then let it stand.
cells.core:
You hold a piece of what you know and you've stopped handing it over. What's left from here is drifting with whatever carries you, and your quiet reads as agreement you didn't give. What you know hasn't gone anywhere; the offering stopped.

The standing that would have been your way through — the moment you stop, the current returns. It won't run backward through an old room to fetch you. It's here, and so is the choice, already open, saying nothing yet. You're the one who stopped, and you're still the one who could start. One piece, said to one person, is enough to test it.
cells.sheetLine: You hold something to pass on and you've stopped passing it.
cells.verb: to pick the direction, this and not that
cells.place: in the shared meanings and practices handed between people

cells.tense: You are steering with the pen down, in a room you are already writing.
cells.ask: Say 'this is mine' about one thing you carry, out loud, to one person today. Then let it stand.
cells.core:
You're already shaping what the people near you take as true — in what you repeat and what you wave through. But you describe it as if it just happens, as if the room or the times were doing that by themselves.

Standing up for it is steering, and that kind of standing stays yours. Ask someone mildly annoying to guess what yours would say and they'd get it right. You do choose. The mood of a room was mostly you; a practice kept going because of your hand. The direction is running; nobody has called it yours. The next move is small: name one thing you set in motion and call it yours.
cells.sheetLine: The steer is already running. Nobody's heard you claim it.

attempts.check: The draft's temptation is to say the person decides what a group believes, which the record doesn't support; the record holds only that direction is choosing, seated in what's shared. A reader could reasonably say the shared thing already exists and they're just holding it steady, so the read must leave room for that. The asks survive being wrong because each one is a small public act — offering one more, letting one answer sit, naming one piece in an ordinary sentence, letting one piece stand without defending it — worth doing whether or not the read is right. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line about carrying wisdom forward; I've cut it, and the cells say transmission instead of authority, plain.
